results.answer:
Connect the concept to its method, explain why the method works, and retain domain assumptions.

A closed box with a square base and no lid must hold a volume of 32 cubic units; minimize the material used. Let the base side be x and the height be h, so the volume constraint is x^2*h = 32, giving h = 32/x^2. The surface area to minimize is the base plus four sides: S = x^2 + 4*x*h = x^2 + 4*x*(32/x^2) = x^2 + 128/x. The feasible domain is x > 0. Differentiate: S'(x) = 2*x - 128/x^2. Setting this to zero gives 2*x = 128/x^2, so x^3 = 64 and x = 4. Then h = 32/16 = 2. Confirm that x = 4 is a minimum by checking the sign: at x = 3 the derivative is 6 - 128/9, about -8.2, and at x = 5 it is 10 - 128/25, about 4.9, so the derivative changes from negative to positive, which is a minimum. The minimum surface area is 16 + 32 = 48 square units.

After substitution the first derivative locates candidate interior points and the sign of the derivative on each side classifies them: a change from positive to negative indicates a local maximum and a change from negative to positive indicates a local minimum. If the derivative does not change sign at a critical point, the point is neither a maximum nor a minimum. For a closed bounded feasible domain, the extreme value theorem guarantees attainment, so comparing the objective values at the critical points and the endpoints suffices to identify the global extremes. For an open domain the extremes may not be attained, and the honest conclusion is then a supremum or an infimum together with a statement that it is not achieved.

Confusing a local extreme with a global one is the central error at this level; showing that a critical point is a local minimum does not show that no other feasible input does better. A second error is treating an open feasible domain as though the extreme value theorem applied, and reporting a supremum as an attained maximum. A third is substituting the constraint in a way that loses a variable's restriction, for example allowing a negative length after solving for the other side. A fourth is discarding units during the algebra, which can hide a mismatch between the objective and the constraint.

At this level the learner substitutes the constraint into the objective, retains units through the algebra, and explains why the chosen domain is the right one. Eliminating a constraint reduces a problem in several variables to a problem in one variable, which is what makes single-variable calculus applicable. The feasible domain is the image of the physically meaningful inputs after substitution, and it may be open, closed, or half-open depending on whether the endpoints correspond to a degenerate configuration such as a zero side length. A local maximum is an input whose objective value is at least as large as at nearby feasible inputs, while a global maximum compares against every feasible input; the two are different claims and the second does not follow from the first.

Example:
We want to construct a box whose base length is 3 times the base width.  The material used to build the top and bottom cost $10/ft^{2} and the material used to build the sides cost $6/ft^{2}.  If the box must have a volume of 50ft^{3} determine the dimensions that will minimize the cost to build the box.
First, a quick figure (probably not to scale…).

!A sketch of a box.  The height is labeled as “h”, the width (or depth) is labeled as “w” and the length is labeled as “l = 3w”.

We want to minimize the cost of the materials subject to the constraint that the volume must be 50ft^{3}.  Note as well that the cost for each side is just the area of that side times the appropriate cost.

The two functions we’ll be working with here this time are,

            \[\begin{align*}{\mbox{Minimize : }} & C = 10\left( {2lw} \right) + 6\left( {2wh + 2lh} \right)\, = 60{w^2} + 48wh\\ {\mbox{Constraint :}}& 50 = lwh = 3{w^2}h\end{align*}\]

As with the first example, we will solve the constraint for one of the variables and plug this into the cost.  It will definitely be easier to solve the constraint for \(h\) so let’s do that.

              \[h = \frac{{50}}{{3{w^2}}}\]

Plugging this into the cost gives,

            \[C\left( w \right) = 60{w^2} + 48w\left( {\frac{{50}}{{3{w^2}}}} \right) = 60{w^2} + \frac{{800}}{w}\]

Now, let’s get the first and second (we’ll be needing this later…) derivatives,

              \[C'\left( w \right) = 120w - 800{w^{ - 2}} = \frac{{120{w^3} - 800}}{{{w^2}}}\hspace{0.25in}\hspace{0.25in}C''\left( w \right) = 120 + 1600{w^{ - 3}}\]

Now we need the critical point(s) for the cost function.  First, notice that \(w = 0\) is not a critical point.  Clearly the derivative does not exist at \(w = 0\) but then neither does the function and remember that values of \(w\) will only be critical points if the function also exists at that point.  Note that there is also a physical reason to avoid \(w = 0\).  We are constructing a box and it would make no sense to have a zero width of the box.

So it looks like the only critical point will come from determining where the numerator is zero.

              \[120{w^3} - 800 = 0\hspace{0.25in} \Rightarrow \hspace{0.25in}\,\,w = \sqrt{{\frac{{800}}{{120}}}} = \sqrt{{\frac{{20}}{3}}} = 1.8821\]

So, we’ve got a single critical point and we now have to verify that this is in fact the value that will give the absolute minimum cost.

In this case we can’t use Method 1 from above.  First, the function is not continuous at one of the endpoints, \(w = 0\), of our interval of possible values, i.e. \(w > 0\).  Secondly, there is no theoretical upper limit to the width that will give a box with volume of 50 ft^{3}.  If \(w\) is very large then we would just need to make \(h\) very small.

The second method listed above would work here, but that’s going to involve some calculations, not difficult calculations, but more work nonetheless.

The third method however, will work quickly and simply here.  First, we know that whatever the value of \(w\) that we get it will have to be positive and we can see second derivative above that provided \(w > 0\) we will have \(C''\left( w \right) > 0\) and so in the interval of possible optimal values the cost function will always be concave up and so \(w = 1.8821\) must give the absolute minimum cost.

All we need to do now is to find the remaining dimensions.

            \[\begin{align*}w & = 1.8821\\ l & = 3w = 3\left( {1.8821} \right) = 5.6463\\  h & = \frac{{50}}{{3{w^2}}} = \frac{{50}}{{3{{\left( {1.8821} \right)}^2}}} = 4.7050\end{align*}\]

Also, even though it was not asked for, the minimum cost is : \(C\left( {1.8821} \right) = \$ 637.60\).

تابع f(x) = x + 1/x را روی دامنه x > 0 کمینه کن و بیان کن که آیا کمینه به دست می‌آید. مشتق بگیر: f'(x) = 1 - 1/x^2 که در x^2 = 1 صفر است، پس x = 1 روی این دامنه. مشتق دوم f''(x) = 2/x^3 است که برای x > 0 مثبت است و کمینه موضعی در x = 1 با مقدار ۲ را تأیید می‌کند. برای ارتقای این به ادعای مطلق توجه کن که f(x) هنگام نزدیک شدن x به صفر از بالا و هنگام میل x به بی‌نهایت به بی‌نهایت میل می‌کند، پس تابع هدف از بالا کران‌دار نیست. مشتق آن روی 0 < x < 1 منفی و روی x > 1 مثبت است، که مطلق بودن این کمینه را ثابت می‌کند. دامنه باز است، اما با این حال کمینه در x = 1 به دست می‌آید چون آن نقطه درون دامنه قرار دارد. این را با g(x) = x روی x > 0 مقایسه کن که اینفیممش صفر است اما هیچ ورودی شدنی به آن نمی‌رسد؛ همین تفاوت دقیقاً تمایزی است که استدلال پایانی باید حفظ کند.

results.answer:
Give precise definitions, justify the method, and discuss assumptions and limitations without needless complexity.

Minimize f(x) = x + 1/x on the domain x > 0, and state whether the minimum is attained. Differentiate: f'(x) = 1 - 1/x^2, which is zero when x^2 = 1, so x = 1 on this domain. The second derivative is f''(x) = 2/x^3, which is positive for x > 0, confirming a local minimum at x = 1 with value 2. To upgrade this to a global claim, note that f(x) tends to infinity as x approaches 0 from above and as x tends to infinity, so the objective is unbounded above, not bounded. Its derivative is negative on 0 < x < 1 and positive on x > 1, proving that this minimum is global. The domain is open, but the minimum is nonetheless attained at x = 1 because that point lies inside the domain. Contrast this with g(x) = x on x > 0, where the infimum is 0 but no feasible input attains it; that difference is exactly the distinction the exit reasoning must preserve.

A vanishing derivative is a necessary condition for an interior local extremum of a differentiable objective, not a sufficient one, and it says nothing at all about the boundary. For a continuous objective on a closed bounded feasible interval the complete candidate set is the interior critical points together with the endpoints, and comparing the objective values across that set, when it is finite identifies the global extremes; this comparison is what upgrades a local claim to a global one. When the feasible set is unbounded, a global minimum may fail to exist even though the objective is bounded below, and the difference between the infimum and the minimum must be reported honestly rather than glossed over. Every claim about optimality should name the feasible set over which it holds, because the same objective can have different optima on different domains. A stationary point need not be either extremum: f(x) = x^3 has f'(0) = 0 but is increasing through zero, so zero is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.

Example:
We have a piece of cardboard that is 14 inches by 10 inches and we’re going to cut out the corners as shown below and fold up the sides to form a box, also shown below.  Determine the height of the box that will give a maximum volume.

!Two sketches side by side with an arrow pointing from the left sketch to the right one.  On the left is the flat piece of cardboard, 14 inches wide and 10 inches tall, with a small square cut out of each of the four corners and dashed fold lines marked.  On the right is the open-topped box that results when the four sides are folded up.
Let’s let the height of the box be \(h\).  So, the width/length of the corners being cut out is also \(h\) and so the vertical side will have a “new” height of \(10 - 2h\) and the horizontal side will have a “new” width of \(14 - 2h\).  Here is a sketch with all this information put in,

!This sketch has two pieces to it.  On the right is a box where the height is labeled as “h”, the width (or depth) is labeled as “10-2h” and the length is labeled as “14-2h”.  On the left is the rectangular piece of cardboard that was used to construct the box.  Interior to this rectangle is another rectangle that will become the bottom of the box.  In each order there are squares, with sides labeled as “h” that are indicated with dashed lines.  These are the squares that must be cut out of the rectangle in order to fold up the remaining pieces to become the sides of the box.  The middle portion of the left side of the rectangle (i.e. the portion between the two “cut out” squares) is labeled “10-2h”.  The middle portion of the bottom side of the rectangle (i.e. the portion between the two “cut out” squares) is labeled “14-2h”.

In this example, for the first time, we’ve run into a problem where the constraint doesn’t really have an equation.  The constraint is simply the size of the piece of cardboard and has already been factored into the figure above.  This will happen on occasion and so don’t get excited about it when it does.  This just means that we have one less equation to worry about. In this case we want to maximize the volume. Here is the volume, in terms of \(h\) and its first derivative.

          \[V\left( h \right) = h\left( {14 - 2h} \right)\left( {10 - 2h} \right) = 140h - 48{h^2} + 4{h^3}\hspace{0.25in}\hspace{0.25in}V'\left( h \right) = 140 - 96h + 12{h^2}\]

Setting the first derivative equal to zero and solving gives the following two critical points,

          \[h = \frac{{12 \pm \sqrt {39} }}{3} = 1.9183,\,\,\,\,6.0817\]

We now have an apparent problem.  We have two critical points and we’ll need to determine which one is the value we need.  The fact that we have two critical points means that neither the first derivative test or the second derivative test can be used here as they both require a single critical point.  This isn’t a real problem however.  Go back to the figure at the start of the solution and notice that we can quite easily find limits on \(h\).  The smallest \(h\) can be is \(h = 0\) even though this doesn’t make much sense as we won’t get a box in this case.  Also, from the 10 inch side we can see that the largest \(h\) can be is \(h = 5\) although again, this doesn’t make much sense physically.

So, knowing that whatever \(h\) is it must be in the range \(0 \le h \le 5\) we can see that the second critical point is outside this range and so the only critical point that we need to worry about is 1.9183.

Finally, since the volume is defined and continuous on \(0 \le h \le 5\) all we need to do is plug in the critical points and endpoints into the volume to determine which gives the largest volume.  Here are those function evaluations.

            \[V\left( 0 \right) = 0\hspace{0.25in}\hspace{0.25in}V\left( {1.9183} \right) = 120.1644\hspace{0.25in}\hspace{0.25in}V\left( 5 \right) = 0\]

So, if we take \(h = 1.9183\) we get a maximum volume.

صفر بودن مشتق شرطی لازم برای اکسترمم موضعی درونی یک هدف مشتق‌پذیر است نه شرطی کافی، و درباره مرز هیچ نمی‌گوید. برای هدف پیوسته روی بازه شدنی بسته و کران‌دار مجموعه کامل کاندیداها نقاط بحرانی درونی به‌همراه سرهاست و مقایسه مقادیر هدف روی این مجموعه، هنگامی که متناهی باشد، اکسترمم‌های مطلق را مشخص می‌کند؛ همین مقایسه است که ادعای موضعی را به ادعای مطلق ارتقا می‌دهد. هنگامی که مجموعه شدنی کران‌دار نباشد، ممکن است کمینه مطلق وجود نداشته باشد حتی اگر تابع هدف از پایین کران‌دار باشد، و تفاوت میان اینفیمم و کمینه باید صادقانه گزارش شود نه پوشانده. هر ادعای بهینگی باید مجموعه شدنی‌ای را که در آن برقرار است نام ببرد، چون تابع هدف یکسان می‌تواند روی دامنه‌های مختلف بهینه‌های متفاوت داشته باشد. ادعای اکسترمم بودن هر نقطه ایستا نادرست است: f(x) = x^3 دارای f'(0) = 0 است اما از صفر به‌صورت افزایشی عبور می‌کند، پس صفر نه بیشینه موضعی است نه کمینه موضعی و هیچ‌کدام نیست.

ارائه نقطه بحرانی به‌عنوان بهینه مطلق بدون مقایسه یا استدلال یکنوایی خطایی است که ادعای مطلق را بی‌پشتوانه می‌گذارد. خطای دوم نادیده گرفتن مرز مجموعه شدنی است، جایی که بهینه مقید اغلب قرار دارد. خطای سوم گزارش اینفیمم به‌عنوان کمینه هنگامی است که مجموعه شدنی باز یا کران‌دار نباشد و مقدار به دست نیاید. خطای چهارم کامل پنداشتن یک محاسبه مشتق است؛ یافتن کاندیداها یک گام است و گام‌های باقی‌مانده دسته‌بندی، بررسی مرز و مقایسه مطلق هستند.

در این سطح یادگیرنده بهینگی مطلق را توجیه می‌کند، مرز ناحیه شدنی را بررسی می‌کند و بیان می‌کند که آیا بهترین مقدار واقعاً به دست می‌آید یا نه. کمینه مطلق در x* به دست می‌آید هرگاه مقدار هدف در آن حداکثر به اندازه مقدار در هر ورودی شدنی باشد و وجود چنین نقطه‌ای پرسشی جدا از یافتن آن است. قضیه مقدار اکسترمم وجود را برای تابع هدفی پیوسته روی مجموعه شدنی ناتهی و فشرده تضمین می‌کند که در یک بُعد یعنی بازه بسته و کران‌دار؛ بیرون آن فرض‌ها وجود باید جداگانه استدلال شود، مثلاً با استدلال یکنوایی یا هم‌کرانی. مرز مجموعه شدنی جایی است که قیدها فعال می‌شوند و باید بررسی شود چون بهینه ممکن است آنجا باشد نه در نقطه بحرانی درونی.

تابع f(x) = x + 1/x را روی دامنه x > 0 کمینه کن و بیان کن که آیا کمینه به دست می‌آید. مشتق بگیر: f'(x) = 1 - 1/x^2 که در x^2 = 1 صفر است، پس x = 1 روی این دامنه. مشتق دوم f''(x) = 2/x^3 است که برای x > 0 مثبت است و کمینه موضعی در x = 1 با مقدار ۲ را تأیید می‌کند. برای ارتقای این به ادعای مطلق توجه کن که f(x) هنگام نزدیک شدن x به صفر از بالا و هنگام میل x به بی‌نهایت به بی‌نهایت میل می‌کند، پس تابع هدف از بالا کران‌دار نیست. مشتق آن روی 0 < x < 1 منفی و روی x > 1 مثبت است، که مطلق بودن این کمینه را ثابت می‌کند. دامنه باز است، اما با این حال کمینه در x = 1 به دست می‌آید چون آن نقطه درون دامنه قرار دارد. این را با g(x) = x روی x > 0 مقایسه کن که اینفیممش صفر است اما هیچ ورودی شدنی به آن نمی‌رسد؛ همین تفاوت دقیقاً تمایزی است که استدلال پایانی باید حفظ کند.

Give precise definitions, justify the method, and discuss assumptions and limitations without needless complexity.

A vanishing derivative is a necessary condition for an interior local extremum of a differentiable objective, not a sufficient one, and it says nothing at all about the boundary. For a continuous objective on a closed bounded feasible interval the complete candidate set is the interior critical points together with the endpoints, and comparing the objective values across that set, when it is finite identifies the global extremes; this comparison is what upgrades a local claim to a global one. When the feasible set is unbounded, a global minimum may fail to exist even though the objective is bounded below, and the difference between the infimum and the minimum must be reported honestly rather than glossed over. Every claim about optimality should name the feasible set over which it holds, because the same objective can have different optima on different domains. A stationary point need not be either extremum: f(x) = x^3 has f'(0) = 0 but is increasing through zero, so zero is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.

Minimize f(x) = x + 1/x on the domain x > 0, and state whether the minimum is attained. Differentiate: f'(x) = 1 - 1/x^2, which is zero when x^2 = 1, so x = 1 on this domain. The second derivative is f''(x) = 2/x^3, which is positive for x > 0, confirming a local minimum at x = 1 with value 2. To upgrade this to a global claim, note that f(x) tends to infinity as x approaches 0 from above and as x tends to infinity, so the objective is unbounded above, not bounded. Its derivative is negative on 0 < x < 1 and positive on x > 1, proving that this minimum is global. The domain is open, but the minimum is nonetheless attained at x = 1 because that point lies inside the domain. Contrast this with g(x) = x on x > 0, where the infimum is 0 but no feasible input attains it; that difference is exactly the distinction the exit reasoning must preserve.

Presenting a critical point as the global optimum without a comparison or a monotonicity argument is the error that leaves the global claim unsupported. A second is ignoring the boundary of the feasible set, where a constrained optimum often lies. A third is reporting an infimum as a minimum when the feasible set is open or unbounded and the value is not attained. A fourth is treating a derivative calculation as a complete solution; locating candidates is one step, and the remaining steps are classification, boundary examination, and the global comparison.

Example:
A printer needs to make a poster that will have a total area of 200 in^{2} and will have 1 inch margins on the sides, a 2 inch margin on the top and a 1.5 inch margin on the bottom as shown below.  What dimensions will give the largest printed area?

!A sketch of the poster.  The outer rectangle is the whole poster and an inner rectangle shows the printed area.  The gap between them is labeled as a 2 inch margin across the top, a 1.5 inch margin across the bottom and a 1 inch margin on each of the left and right sides.
This problem is a little different from the previous problems.  Both the constraint and the function we are going to optimize are areas.  The constraint is that the overall area of the poster must be 200 in^{2} while we want to optimize the printed area (i.e. the area of the poster with the margins taken out).

Let’s define the height of the poster to be \(h\) and the width of the poster to be \(w\).  Here is a new sketch of the poster and we can see that once we’ve taken the margins into account the width of the printed area is \(w - 2\) and the height of the printer area is \(h - 3.5\).

!This is a rectangle with another rectangle sketched inside it.  The inner rectangle represents the area that will actually be printed.  The height of the outer rectangle is labeled “h” and the width of outer rectangle is labeled “w”.  The distance between the right/left sides of the outer rectangle and inner rectangle are labeled “1 inch margin”.  The distance between the tops of the two rectangles is labeled “2 inch margin”.  The distance between the bottoms of the two rectangles is labeled “1.5 inch margin”.   The height of the inner rectangle is labeled “h-3.5” and the width of the inner rectangle is labeled “w-2”.

Here are the equations that we’ll be working with.

            \[\begin{align*}{\mbox{Maximize : }} & A = \left( {w - 2} \right)\left( {h - 3.5} \right)\\ {\mbox{Constraint :}} & 200 = wh\end{align*}\]

Solving the constraint for \(h\) and plugging into the equation for the printed area gives,

            \[A\left( w \right) = \left( {w - 2} \right)\left( {\frac{{200}}{w} - 3.5} \right) = 207 - 3.5w - \frac{{400}}{w}\]

The first and second derivatives are,

          \[A'\left( w \right) =  - 3.5 + \frac{{400}}{{{w^2}}} = \frac{{400 - 3.5{w^2}}}{{{w^2}}}\hspace{0.25in}\hspace{0.25in}A''\left( w \right) =  - \frac{{800}}{{{w^3}}}\]

From the first derivative we have the following two critical points (\(w = 0\) is not a critical point because the area function does not exist there).

            \[w =  \pm \,\sqrt {\frac{400}{3.5}}  =  \pm \,10.6904\]

However, since we’re dealing with the dimensions of a piece of paper we know that we must have \(w > 0\) and so only 10.6904 will make sense.

Also notice that provided \(w > 0\) the second derivative will always be negative and so in the range of possible optimal values of the width the area function is always concave down and so we know that the maximum printed area will be at \(w = 10.6904\,\,{\mbox{inches}}\).

The height of the paper that gives the maximum printed area is then,

            \[h = \frac{{200}}{{10.6904}} = 18.7084\,\,{\mbox{inches}}\]
